item.itunes:title: OpenAI killing Atlas pushed me to a local AI browser setup, and I should have made the switch much sooner
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When OpenAI announced in July that ChatGPT Atlas would stop working in August 2026, less than a year after its October 2025 launch, the shutdown was less surprising than the timing. Nine months from launch to sunset for a browser that was supposed to be OpenAI's big play at Chrome, folded back into the ChatGPT desktop app and a Chrome extension instead.

Many of the AI tools I've watched come and go over the past two years have followed a similar route. There's usually some big launch, a lot of hype and tutorials and reviews, then like clockwork there's a blog post explaining that the team is being redirected somewhere else. I already run a portion of my AI stack on local models for exactly this reason, though I haven't extended that to my browser yet, until recently.

The AI graveyard is getting a little crowded

Atlas is not the first, and it won't be the last

Atlas itself is the cleanest recent example. OpenAI launched it in October 2025 as a new agentic browser built around ChatGPT, then confirmed the sunset for August 9, 2026, nine months in. The official framing was that the features would live on inside the ChatGPT desktop app and a Chrome extension, though internally OpenAI's leadership had been telling teams to cut what they called "side quests" for months.

This is the same reason Sora got shut down back in April, which left mid-project creators unable to access videos they'd already generated. To be fair, Atlas did earn some of its ending, with prompt injection vulnerabilities documented, and one test also clocked the agent at ten full minutes to add three items to an Amazon cart.

Arc is another one, and a browser I'd heard designers talk about non-stop a while back. The Browser Company put it into maintenance mode in May 2025 and pivoted the whole team to a new AI-first browser called Dia, and then Atlassian bought the company for $610 million in October. Arc still runs but nobody's building it anymore, and the source code stayed closed because it shares an SDK with Dia.

And even the tools that don't fully shut down don't really sit still - OpenAI killed GPT-4o inside ChatGPT this February and a Change.org petition with more than 20,000 signatures didn't bring it back. I don't think any of this is out of malice, it's just incentives that control the situation.

OpenAI is merging ChatGPT, Codex, and its browser into one superapp

It's a sign the company is finally getting focused.

By  Simon Batt

Why use local AI in the browser at all?

When the browser itself is already online

My browser is a cloud thing by definition; it talks to remote servers all day, logs me into accounts, and syncs my history. So what does swapping out the AI layer for a local model actually change? The distinction, I think, is between the browser's normal traffic and the AI layer sitting on top of it.

Normal traffic goes to sites I've already decided to trust, or at least tolerate. The AI layer is a different thing because it sees everything at once, including the page I'm reading, the doc I've asked it to summarize, and the prompt itself where I've explained what I'm actually trying to do with it.

That's the part I want on my own machine. So when I run a local model through BrowserOS pointed at LM Studio, the contents of every AI conversation just stay on my SSD, my prompts aren't training data for anyone, and if either BrowserOS or LM Studio ever gets shut down, I've still got my past chats.

Local isn't the answer to everything though. Ad tracking, ISP visibility, and fingerprinting are all separate problems that come down to which browser you pick in the first place. There's also a capability issue; BrowserOS's own docs say local models handle Chat Mode well but aren't yet powerful enough for Agent Mode, which needs a bigger brain to reliably click the right elements across multi-step tasks. I've been doing just fine without Agent Mode, however.

I hooked up my AI browser to a local LLM and it finally solved my biggest problem

When you stop letting your browser AI phone home

By  Nolen Jonker

My setup (and the alternatives worth knowing)

It took five minutes to set up

My setup is pretty boring, with BrowserOS as my browser, LM Studio running a local model as an OpenAI-compatible server, and the browser pointed at that endpoint. If you're interested in switching to BrowserOS, it lets you import Chrome data since it's a Chromium fork, so your bookmarks, passwords, and extensions can carry over smoothly.

I prefer BrowserOS specifically because it treats local as a first-class option rather than an afterthought. It also works on Windows, Mac, and Linux, with built-in MCP support for Gmail and Docs and a handful of other useful nuggets. And if the company behind it vanished tomorrow, the code's public and someone could fork it, which is the actual insurance policy against everything I was just complaining about.

Brave is the other one I'd recommend for local AI chat. Leo's Bring Your Own Model feature hits any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so LM Studio and Ollama both plug in smoothly. The only downside is that the "Answer with AI" button in Brave Search itself doesn't route through your local model, only the Leo sidebar does. Then there's also Opera. It was actually the first mainstream browser to ship built-in local LLM support back in April 2024. Opera One now covers over 2000 model variants through the Ollama framework.

I've been using Chrome for a decade, and one week of Comet convinced me to switch

Chrome is still catching up to where Comet already is

By  Nolen Jonker

My AI browser can't be sunset, sold, or gutted in a policy update

Watching Atlas vanish is what ultimately pushed me to start bringing local AI to my browser workflows, and also choose more reliable and open browsers. Every AI tool you don't own is basically on a clock, whether it's a browser or a video model. So it might be worth looking into ways you can make pieces of your AI stack more your own.

item.title: I starting using a projector as my only TV, and it changed how I watch everything
item.itunes:title: I starting using a projector as my only TV, and it changed how I watch everything
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When I renovated my home a few months back, I decided to drop the big television hogging space on the wall. In fact, I don't have a television at all anymore. Instead, I use a portable projector because, for the way I consume media, it solves several problems that a conventional TV simply can't.

The biggest one is the simplest — I don't want a giant black rectangle permanently mounted on the wall when I'm not actively watching something. My projector, however, simply disappears out of view. I can chuck it in a cabinet or on a shelf, and bring it out only when I actually want to watch something. That small change makes a massive difference in how my room feels, making it feel less like it is built around the screen.

More importantly, it gives me flexibility to decide where and how I want to watch a movie. While a television means plonking myself in the living room, the projector lets me throw an impromptu movie night on the terrace, or set up a cozy viewing experience in the bedroom on a cold winter night.

A projector elevates every movie night

Bigger, more flexible screens make a big difference

The most obvious use case is the one that convinced me that this setup is perfect for me. When I'm getting ready to watch a movie, ease of access is paramount. I pick up my projector from my shelf, point it at the wall, and turn it on. That's it. Modern portable projectors have made setup and start incredibly easy.

Autofocus and automatic keystone correction have taken care of much of the fiddling that came with setting up a projector. I no longer need to spend five to ten minutes adjusting the lens and trying to get a perfectly aligned image. That makes a big difference in everyday use. While it might seem like the extra step of picking up the projector from the shelf adds friction, in everyday use it's a minor inconvenience that pales in comparison to the advantages here.

The other aspect of using projectors is dealing with projector screens. Well, I don't use one. A reasonably clean, light-colored wall works more than well enough for everyday viewing. Would I benefit from an ALR screen? Probably. But I'm not watching cinematic masterpieces every day. The average flick looks better on a massive screen if the color isn't quite as punchy as an OLED screen.

And that brings me to size. Contrary to popular opinion, when it comes to projectors and movie viewing, size matters. A projector allows for a much larger screen than I could get with a regular television. Not just that, the screen is completely flexible to my needs. So I place the projector a bit closer when I'm in my bedroom, and it gives me a more compact 49-inch TV-style experience. Meanwhile, the living room gets a full 120-inches. It's great.

The flexibility of having a projector means I'm always looking for opportunities to put it to interesting new uses. For example, recently I had some friends over to watch football. With the weather unusually good, we decided to pop out into the garden and project the match onto the wall while setting up the barbecue. Was it picture perfect? No. But the experience was unmatched by any television.

Another aspect worth mentioning is that most modern projectors, especially portable ones, come with built-in smarts. With Google TV support, I don't really need to plug in a streaming stick. Everything is built in. I've signed in to my Netflix and YouTube accounts, and I can watch those streams from anywhere. In fact, on occasion I've carried my projector to a friend's home, logged into the Wi-Fi network, and continued watching. Try doing that with a TV.

Of course, the built-in HDMI ports get used too. The experience of playing a blockbuster game like the recent James Bond title on a 100-inch screen is absolutely unmatched. It goes without saying that no setup is perfect. And a projector certainly comes with some compromises. If you tend to watch a lot of TV in a brightly lit room, this isn't the setup for you. A portable projector doesn't get bright enough to handle that.

Audio is another thing to keep in mind. While speakers have generally gotten better, the dinky little speakers built into a projector certainly aren't going to replace a home theater system. Investing in a decent set of speakers greatly elevates the experience. As for me, I usually pair it with Bluetooth speakers or headphones.

Why I prefer a projector over a television

A television is obviously the simpler choice for most. After all, you can't really beat pressing a button and getting on with your media consumption. But a projector opens up options. You can move it around, change the screen size at will, and even carry it with you. If you value those benefits, a projector will easily win out for you, as it has for me. In fact, going back to a regular television feels surprisingly restrictive once you're used to a setup like this.

item.title: 6 things I keep open next to my code editor, and they make my workflow productive
item.itunes:title: 6 things I keep open next to my code editor, and they make my workflow productive
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When I sit down to code, my editor takes up most of the screen, but it’s never working alone. Over time, I’ve built a small lineup of apps that I keep open throughout the day. They help me handle the different parts of development without turning my desktop into a sea of browser tabs. I don’t open these apps because they look impressive or promise better productivity. They’re simply tools I’ve found useful enough to keep around every time I code.

Notes app is always within reach

My ideas need a home too

I keep Obsidian open next to my code editor because I’m constantly thinking of things that I don’t want to lose. It might be a quick idea for something I want to build, a solution I want to try later, or a thought that comes to me while I’m working. I’d rather write it down immediately than trust myself to remember it.

Obsidian works well for this because I can keep my notes simple and organized without turning note-taking into another complicated task. I have separate notes for different ideas, and I can quickly jump between them when I need to. It has become the place where I put thoughts that are useful but don’t belong in my code or editor.

Task manager keeps my day on track

My day stays on the rails

Asana stays open because my workday includes more than the code I’m currently writing. I use it to keep track of what I need to finish, what I’m waiting on, and what I want to tackle next. Having that list visible helps me stay focused without trying to remember every small responsibility in my head.

I like being able to break larger pieces of work into smaller tasks and mark them off as I go. It gives me a clear sense of progress, especially on days when I’m working on several things at once. I also use due dates when something needs to be finished by a specific time. For me, Asana is simply a reliable place to see what needs my attention.

PDF reader handles the documents I actually need

For those PDFs I keep checking

SumatraPDF stays open because I regularly need to check PDFs while I’m working. These can be manuals, guides, specifications, or other reference documents. I keep it beside my code editor so I can quickly switch to a document when I need to verify something.

I often use it to search through longer documents, jump between pages, and keep a reference open while I continue working. It also supports several common document formats, which means I don’t need a separate app for every file I come across. I don’t use my PDF reader constantly, but I like having it ready when I need it. It saves me from interrupting my workflow just to open and check a document.

The fastest way to test endpoints

I also find it useful for understanding the bigger picture of a page. I can look at different screens and see how the interface is supposed to work together. My editor has plenty of company

I used to think I needed a browser open beside my editor for almost everything. Now, I’ve realized that a good coding setup is more about having the right tools within reach. Each app on my desktop has a clear purpose, and together they make my workday feel more organized. I don’t need dozens of tabs competing for my attention. Sometimes, keeping the browser out of the way is exactly what helps me stay focused on the work in front of me.

item.title: Smart pet gadgets are overpriced, so I built one from a $15 sensor and local automation
item.itunes:title: Smart pet gadgets are overpriced, so I built one from a $15 sensor and local automation
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Smart products exist in pretty much every single product category, including for your pets. When I looked at a smart terrarium controller for my gecko, I noticed it easily ran me between $80 and $150. Most were clunky, relied on proprietary, ad-ridden cloud apps, connected over flaky 2.4GHz Wi-Fi blobs, and featured primitive on/off logic that wears out hardware.

Instead of an ugly, expensive proprietary hub, I chose an unassuming $15 SwitchBot sensor stuck to the inside. Behind the display is a precision temperature and humidity sensor that broadcasts the telemetry I need. Ingesting those packets locally into Home Assistant unlocks true industrial control paradigms. I didn't need dedicated cloud-tethered pet gadgets to build an environmental control system by intercepting passive BLE advertisements with an ESPHome Bluetooth proxy and building closed-loop generic thermostat and hygrostat state machines into Home Assistant. An ordinary $15 sensor became a resilient enterprise-grade climate controller.

I can now slap my table to turn on my PC, thanks to a simple vibration sensor

With an ESP32 and a simple sensor, I can slap my table to turn on my PC for less than $5.

7
By  Adam Conway

You can use a sensor without a hub at all

Thanks to BLE

When you pick up a SwitchBot sensor, it works with Matter, but many enthusiasts don't take advantage of a BLE architecture. You don't need the cloud, and you don't need a hub. It's a result of passive advertisement sniffing.

The SwitchBot protocol means that the sensor does not require an active, battery-draining two-way GATT connection. It continuously broadcasts open Bluetooth Low Energy, or BLE, advertisement packets containing raw hexadecimal payloads encoding temperature, relative humidity, and battery voltage. This means you can pair it with a $4 ESPHome Bluetooth proxy pipeline.

Thick terrarium glass, water misting, and even the room's walls can degrade Bluetooth range to a central server. By placing a cheap ESP32 board running ESP Home's Bluetooth proxy near the enclosure, this creates a local radio bridge. It passively sniffs Switchport BLE packets and relays the telemetry over local Wi-Fi or Ethernet straight to Home Assistant via the native API.

The payoff means you get sub-second response latency, zero internet dependency, zero cloud subscription fees, and a 2-year sensor battery life.

Be sure you set up automations correctly

Don't let your devices cycle

When setting up automations to pair with my sensor, many standard smart home automations fail in delicate biological environments, but industrial control loops can fix them.

For example, if you use a standard native automation like "if humidity is less than 70%, turn on the mister, and if humidity is greater than or equal to 70%, turn off the mister," this can lead to a mechanical failure. A sensor fluctuating between 69.9% and 70.1% can cause rapid relay chatter, cycling a mechanical smart plug or solenoid valve to arc, weld, or burn out the pump motor dozens of times an hour.

The solution here is to instead take advantage of deadband engineering. By implementing Home Assistant's native generic humidistat and generic thermostat integrations, you can configure a strict target tolerance. For example, you can target 72% with a tolerance of three. This means the mister engages only when humidity drops below 69% and runs until it reaches 75%, allowing the system to rest and preventing micro-cycling.

A dead man's switch is essential

Don't let your automation cause problems

It's so fundamental, if you're implementing something like this, that you have life-saving fail-safes. Essentially, you need an out-of-band dead man switch. Since you're controlling a live animal habitat, the ethical and hardware safety engineering is required. Cheap proportional thermostats and smart plugs running inductive ceramic heat emitters or deep heat projectors can suffer from contact welding when stuck in the permanently on state. You need to make sure you have a bit of dual-layer architecture.

The first layer should be the primary controller. The primary thermostat loop regulates day/night basking via a dimmer or solid-state relay.

Layer 2 should be the outer band hardware breaker. The SwitchBot sensor acts as an independent watchdog. If the temperature ever exceeds a critical safety threshold (for example, over 31°C for a cold-tolerant gecko), an emergency automation hard-cuts power to the entire circuit via an upstream smart breaker plug, blares an alert on phone speakers, and broadcasts a high-priority TTS warning to desktop workstations. That way, you're notified immediately if something goes wrong and could put your pet in danger.

Switchbot Smart Room Thermometer Hygrometer Sensor Plus

The Smart Room Thermometer Hygrometer Sensor Plus is great for those who want a simple sensor.

See at Amazon

Smart devices don't always need to be smart by nature

Turn your normal devices into smart devices

Building a bulletproof smart home isn't about buying devices labeled "smart" by marketing departments. An inexpensive temperature sensor broadcasting raw bytes over Bluetooth when connected to an open local engine can deliver high precision, strong safety, and better reliability than commercial hardware that costs 10 times as much. Instead of overpaying for closed-ecosystem smart gadgets, you can stick a $15 sensor anywhere in your home, drop an ESP32 on your desk, and configure it based on your needs.

item.title: The RTX 5090 loses half its performance to DLSS 5, and Nvidia's favorite trick won't save it this time
item.itunes:title: The RTX 5090 loses half its performance to DLSS 5, and Nvidia's favorite trick won't save it this time
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The highly anticipated (and highly controversial) DLSS 5 is finally out. We've seen some breathtaking implementations, but unfortunately, the benchmarks aren't looking as good. Nvidia's latest neural rendering technology delivers some impressive visual results when it comes to atmosphere, characters and objects with respect to tone and depth, but getting there comes with a hefty performance cost that could drive enthusiasts away rather than luring them in.

As a matter of fact, the performance hit is so massive that even Nvidia's favorite trick in the book, Frame Generation, could potentially not be able to salvage it this time. There's a structural reason for that, and it's part of these benchmarks that should worry Blackwell GPU owners, even the ones with a flagship RTX 5090.

The first official DLSS 5 game brought the RTX 5090 to its knees

That might just be a brand-new sentence

The visual results of DLSS 5 were impressive, and reviewers with hands-on time on early DLSS 5 builds, myself included, have generally come away rather fascinated with what neural rendering can do to a scene.

Right now, NBA 2K27 is the only title with official DLSS 5 support, and Nvidia dropped the accompanying driver update on September 3 ahead of the launch. Digital Foundry's coverage of the implementation concedes that it was subtle and tasteful, at least as far as visuals are concerned. On the performance side of things, however, the story becomes a lot less flattering and raises more questions than it answers.

In DF's benchmark runs, the incumbent flagship RTX 5090 fell from 128.4 FPS at 4K resolution down to 62.7 FPS with DLSS 5 enabled, measuring a 51.2% drop on the fastest consumer graphics card on sale. What's even more interesting is that the flagship is not the worst case here.

Credit: Digital Foundry.

The RTX 5080 suffered from a 58.4% performance hit at 4K, landing at 42.6 FPS, sitting uncomfortably below the 60 FPS floor. On the cheapest Blackwell card, the hit was the mildest on the board, however, DF ran it at high rather than ultra preset at 1080p resolution. TechSpot's analysis found a reasonable explanation for this, stating that DLSS 5 likely has a fixed cost that's dependent on the output resolution, which makes sense when you look at the performance data from the RTX 5060 run.

I tried running games at native resolution again, but DLSS 4.5 changed my mind

Even pixel peepers would struggle to justify native rendering at this point

29
By  Hamlin Rozario

But the performance hit isn't the only cost

Neural rendering also drinks power like nothing before it

For a feature as compute intensive as DLSS 5, you can bet that there are power draw implications to match it as well. And sure enough, Tom's Hardware's testing confirmed as much, demonstrating that enabling neural-rendering pass can make the Blackwell flagship significantly thirstier, even as frame rates take a nose dive heading for the ground.

It's worth noting that the DLSS 5 build tested by Tom's Hardware was an OptiScaler injection mod similar to my own experiment with DLSS 5, and as such, the publication notes that a developer-implemented version through Nvidia's Streamline framework may incur less overhead than what was measured in their tests.

In Hogwarts Legacy, an MSI Lightning Z RTX 5090 went from 480W with DLSS 5 disabled to 720W with it on, which was a massive 50% jump in consumption. The Founders Edition of the same card, on the other hand, went from 417W to 547W, resulting in a 31% increase. Control, meanwhile, had the Lightning Z card leaping from 691 W to 802W.

Cyberpunk 2077 with path tracing enabled had the FE card drawing 482W without DLSS 5 and only 551W with it, which looks like a mild 14% increase until you take into account that the FE cannot exceed 575W due to a hard power limit. In the same test, the Lightning Z jumped from 580W to 723W.

Frame Generation can't seem to save DLSS 5 from itself

Nvidia's favorite trick may salvage the frame rates, but what can it do for latency?

So far, all testing points to the fact that DLSS 5 costs more power, inevitably produces more heat as a result, and has a chance of pushing certain SKUs well past what their rated 12V-2x6 connectors are designed to sustain, all while frame rates halve on the same hardware. Whether the visual uplift alone warrants that cost is yet to be answered.

Now, of course, the obvious question that's raised is that, since it's Nvidia, and one of Blackwell's defining features is 6x Multi-Frame Generation, surely it would be able to salvage some of that performance, right? Well, not quite. Digital Foundry's Oliver McKenzie explained that, because of where the model sits, it gets a little more complicated. DLSS 5 runs after upscaling but before frame generation, which means the base frame rate MFG has to interpolate from is the post-DLSS-5 figure, and not the pre-DLSS-5 one.

MFG can certainly lift the counter from there, but then the next issue becomes latency. Digital Foundry measured around 50–60 ms of PC latency on the 5090 with 4x MFG active, and over 60–70 ms on the 5080 and 5060. This is quite different from running MFG stacked on a healthy base frame rate, which is precisely where Nvidia pitched that the technology would shine.

Nvidia’s DLSS 4.5 is a huge visual upgrade, but there’s a catch

It's a cost not everyone would be comfortable paying.

6
By  Samarveer Singh

It's clear that, in its current state, the Blackwell lineup isn't ready for an enjoyable gaming experience with neural rendering.

More power consumption, fewer frames, and for what?

It's clear that, in its current state, the Blackwell lineup isn't ready for an enjoyable gaming experience with neural rendering. This puts Team Green in a rather awkward position surrounding a feature set that was deeply unpopular to begin with, and when the very same feature asks requires more power and generates fewer frames, it becomes a tough sell.

The silver lining, of course, is the fact that it's still very early for DLSS 5, and given enough time and developer effort, it might just become the next big thing. For now, though, I'd stick with DLSS 4.5.

item.title: I wanted Safari’s performance with Chrome’s extensions, and Orion gave me both
item.itunes:title: I wanted Safari’s performance with Chrome’s extensions, and Orion gave me both
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've made no secret of my issues with Chrome. As feature-rich as the browser is, it's an absolute hog on system resources. Opening six tabs shouldn't demand as much RAM as it does, and that strain becomes increasingly apparent on older hardware. Yet in spite of these complaints, I haven't made the jump to Safari because it lacks the robust extension collection that Chrome has, and I can't imagine browsing the web without my favorite suite of tools.

That's when I discovered Orion. This macOS-focused browser has all the efficiency of Safari while boasting the exact extension library as Chrome (with all of Firefox's extensions thrown in, too). Orion is built on Apple's native WebKit instead of Chromium, so it feels like Safari in every way that matters.

Orion has access to more extensions than Chrome

My favorite extensions work surprisingly well

One of Orion's most interesting features is its access (and compatibility with) both the Chrome Web Store and the full collection of Firefox add-ons. In its early days, the browser caught a lot of flak for claiming to support all of these, but users reported that many extensions simply didn't work. That was several years ago, and now Kagi — the developers behind Orion — say that the WebKit API offers roughly 70% extension compatibility.

As Kagi points out, that's a Herculean effort. Many of these extensions were coded to work on Chromium, not WebKit, so the fact that the team has ported so many by hand is a testament to the work they've put into this browser. After testing it for a while, I'm impressed. While there are some extensions that don't work, I haven't personally run into any. The extensions I use, like Proton Pass, uBlock Origin, and Bonjourr, all work seamlessly.

That said, there are some extensions that will just be incompatible. If the extension centers on an API that's no longer maintained or supported, the only way to get it to work would be rebuilding it from the ground up.

This non-Chromium Linux browser can run Chrome, Firefox, and Safari extensions

It's still in beta, but worth a look.

4
By  Simon Batt

Its day-to-day use feels like Safari

The browser is fast, responsive, and familiar

Orion looks like Safari, but given their shared DNA, that makes sense. More importantly, however, is that it performs like Safari. Web pages are snappier, navigation feels smoother, and switching between tabs is instant. That's a far cry from the performance I receive on Chrome, where switching between tabs can take a second or more if I have too many open at once.

That's not to say Orion is faster than Safari. I've compared the two under similar conditions, but I couldn't tell enough of a difference between them to decide a winner. Its performance is at least as fast as Safari, which means Orion meets the main reason I considered switching browsers in the first place: speed.

Orion has nearly everything I need in a browser

I don't need total feature parity

Orion might not be well known, but it combines Safari's speed and responsiveness with the extension support I want from Chrome. While it might not support everything, the plugins I rely on most all work as I expect. I suspect that the majority of popular plugins have full or near-full support, while the extensions that don't work as well are likely more niche. It might take longer before those receive support in Orion.

Here's the thing: while it doesn't match Chrome feature-for-feature, Orion is close enough that it meets all my needs (aside from a few that are software-specific and outside a browser developer's control). And it doesn't feel like a copy of Chrome, either. Orion feels more like Safari or Opera than Chrome, but distinct enough to feel like its own experience.

I ditched Chrome years ago, here are 5 open-source browsers I recommend instead

There are better options out there

27
By  Anurag Singh

The bad news: Orion has limited availability

The only stable release is for Apple devices

While Orion is quite impressive, it's currently only fully available for macOS, iOS, and iPadOS. There's a public beta available for Linux, and the Windows version is under active development and planned for an initial launch in late 2026. That would mean sometime within the next three months, so not too terribly long a wait. But if you want to use it before then, you'll need to access it through one of its supported platforms.

That said, some users report bugs and crashes even on the stable release. I haven't encountered any yet, but as with any relatively young software, a few obstacles are expected.

It's time for the browser monopoly to end

There are more browser options than ever before, but so many essential tools — especially for independent creatives and freelancers — lean on a Chromium base to function, which means only Chrome and a handful of other browsers are fully compatible. That's one of the reasons I keep using Chrome, but Orion has had a constant spot on my toolbar since I discovered it, and I find myself growing more and more fond of the browser.

Orion

Orion is a WebKit-based browser that supports both Chrome extensions and Firefox add-ons.

item.title: My multi-color 3D prints stopped wasting filament when I gave up on printing large parts in one go
item.itunes:title: My multi-color 3D prints stopped wasting filament when I gave up on printing large parts in one go
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When I got my first FDM 3D printer, I didn’t care all that much about filament purge. Sure, the printer would leave randomly extruded bits of filament to prime the nozzle, but I was more concerned with failed models, as they were the primary source of filament waste for my setup. Multi-color printing, however, is a completely different story, and it wasn't until I tried using an AMS-like module that I finally realized why 3D printing enthusiasts have mixed feelings about these setups.

So, I’ve spent the last couple of months trying out all sorts of optimizations and tricks to limit the amount of waste generated when turning multi-color 3MF files into tangible models with my single-nozzle 3D printer. Among them, splitting large prints into smaller models that I could print separately delivered the best results.

Your 3D printer's default purge settings are designed for safety, not savings

Your 3D printer’s purge defaults protect print quality, but they can waste filament unless you tune them for each color swap.

2
By  Jeff Butts

Filament swaps are a major reason behind all the extra waste in single nozzle printers

Depending on their layers, larger models can easily have thousands of swaps

When it comes to consumer-tier FDM printers that support multi-color modules, you’ll typically find single-nozzle options, which need to constantly purge the melted filament out when switching colors. Essentially, once the printer encounters an instruction for a color swap, it doesn’t print the new filament until the old one is fully flushed out. Otherwise, your models would have different colors bleeding into different layers, ultimately ruining their aesthetics.

The problem is that typical multi-color prints have several color swaps, to the point where a particularly large model like a cosplay prop can require the filament to change thousands of times. This ends up with piles of 3D printer poop that’s practically useless for the average consumer.

Heck, even the pigments of the filament rolls can influence the amount of melted plastic that gets tossed out through the purge chute. Dark-to-light transitions, for example, generate a lot of filament poop, as the darker pigment can leave noticeable tints on the lighter colors and needs to be removed completely to avoid grayish edges. And I’m not just talking about a few extra grams, either. I’ve created certain articulated prints where the purged filament alone needed 150+ grams of a PLA roll, while the model barely required 300 grams.

As if that’s not enough, you’ll also need a purge tower, which is a sacrificial structure that the 3D printer creates just to calibrate the nozzle for a smooth color transition. This, in turn, produces even more filament waste, and turning it off runs the risk of filament swaps ruining your print. Of course, converting any old functional part into a purge tower helps, but I’ve had some prints where I needed such a large model to calibrate the color swaps that I ended up needing more filament for it. Not to mention, the color changes themselves consume extra time, and you could easily be looking at 24+ hour prints on larger models with constant filament purge every few layers.

10 ways to get rid of stringing in your 3D prints

When 3D printing, you might see wisps of filament in your finished product, known as stringing. Here's how to eliminate it.

By  Jeff Butts

Splitting large models into smaller prints reduces the filament purge considerably

The individual models are quicker to print and don’t need a purge tower

My favorite solution to the filament purge conundrum involves breaking down the entire model into more manageable prints that I could print separately and combining them together at the end. And before you strike me down for suggesting it, let me add that I’m well aware that it’s not possible for every model. But if I was trying to print something like a cosplay mask featuring horns and all sorts of colored parts, I’d rather split the parts requiring different colors into separate models.

Take the PLA katana I 3D printed for the bard in our D&D group the other day. Rather than spending days and an ungodly amount of filament attempting to print the whole thing at one go, I created the grip and the blade separately with different colors, and then slotted them together. In fact, Printables, MakerWorld, and other model repositories even have STL files with distinct elements that can be meshed together (oftentimes without needing any glue whatsoever).

The best part? Such a workflow doesn’t need a purge tower, and I can add as many supports to the individual parts without worrying about my filament wastage spiking due to even more color swaps. Sure, my printer would generate some poop when I switch the filament once it’s done creating a specific element of the larger model, but this color swap occurs only a few times, as opposed to hundreds (or even thousands). Likewise, although my 3D printer spends additional time leveling the bed for each component, the overall print time is often less than half of what it’d otherwise take if I tried printing the entire multi-colored model at a go.

But there are some tricks to avoid burning through filament on multi-color prints

If you’ve got articulated models that can’t be split into smaller parts, there are still ways to reduce the amount of filament purged by the printer. Flushing into another object is a great way to get a spare model from all the purged material, though enabling this setting might end up spiking the print times. If you’re trying to print a small model, it’s a good idea to create multiple copies instead of just one, as the total purged filament doesn’t scale with the number of models.

item.title: 4 Plex companion apps that take my media server to the next level
item.itunes:title: 4 Plex companion apps that take my media server to the next level
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When it comes to self-hosted media, Plex is where many people start, since it's straightforward to set up and use. A lot of people are familiar with music companion Plexamp, but may not know about other apps that can enhance their media experience.

Jellyfin users know of the vast array of plugins, clients, and apps available, and testing them out is fun. However, several apps for your Plex server can improve the overall experience in fun, unique ways.

Infuse

A slick UI for Plex on Apple devices

When you watch Plex content with the default client on Apple TV and other devices, it's not the slickest UI for Apple's platform. Instead, you can use Infuse to add the content on your Plex server to a higher-end video player. Infuse is a media player meant for all Apple products, including iPhone, iPad, Mac, and Apple TV. It supports a wide range of video file types that may require server-side transcoding, which can increase the server's workload. It's a perfect companion app for Apple device users.

Not only can you enjoy Plex content on a slicker video player interface, but you can also add local files and connect to other self-hosting media platforms, including Jellyfin and Emby. You can then see most of your media in one central location without relying on individual clients.

It's a slick app and makes it easy to connect your Plex server to the app on all Apple devices. It also provides everything you'd expect from a client, from chapter support to a range of video playback controls, and more.

Infuse
See at Apple
I've stopped recommending Plex to newcomers, because Jellyfin is ready for families now

The gap between the Plex and Jellyfin's polish is no longer a chasm

36
By  Samarveer Singh

Plezy

Access paywalled features

A lot has been said about the irritation Plex users feel over the company putting features behind Plex Pass. Some people have stopped using Plex and switched to Jellyfin or Emby or purchased a lifetime subscription to Pass. Another option is the open-source, cross-platform alternative app Plezy. It provides a Plex-like experience on your devices and includes many features that are behind Plex Pass or missing from regular Plex.

Plezy also does things vanilla Plex can't. Plezy gives you access to the recently paywalled Watch Party feature and offline downloads, which you can set to delete automatically once watched. It also provides credit and intro skipping, which no one who hosts their own media should pay for.

Plus, for good measure, it includes broader codec support to help ease the server's workload and variable-speed playback in the player controls. It also has a ton of settings, so you can tweak Plezy to fit your media needs specifically on a per-device basis.

Plezy
See at Github

QuasiTV

Turn your library into a streaming TV guide

Are you tired of scrolling endlessly through your Plex media library for something to watch? The QuasiTV app turns your Plex media library into a TV guide. Just like you used to on cable or still do on free live-streaming services like Pluto TV or The Roku Channel. But this isn't for random FAST streaming channels; it's a listing guide for the titles in your Plex library. It also works with Jellyfin and Emby servers.

Your library layout isn't the unique thing here. Shows and movies are scheduled when they're available. It's a great option when I can't decide what to watch. It is a free app available for Android TV from the Play Store and Fire TV via the Amazon Appstore — there's no sideloading necessary.

QuasiTV is straightforward to set up, and once you connect to your Plex server, you'll have an instant old-school menu system to channel surf your self-hosted media.

QuasiTV
See at Amazon Appstore See at Google Play Store

Tautulli

Find out more about your Plex server

This app is for self-hosting media enthusiasts who want the nerdy stats about their server that Plex doesn't show so that they can fix problems. Tautulli shows more server activity details than the Plex dashboard displays.

It lets me see detailed logs to track usage and monitor server activity. It helps me troubleshoot buffering and other playback issues. The app works on mobile and desktop, so I can monitor what the server is doing from virtually anywhere.

It shows important items like user activity logs — timestamps, time logged on, etc. It also shows media file playback details, bandwidth usage, server analytics, and other advanced information. Another helpful feature is seeing if Direct Play works across multiple devices for a file. Tautulli is a must-have companion app if you are serious about administering your server.

Tautulli
See at Google Play Store See at Github

Jellyfin gets companion app praise, but Plex has them too

Jellyfin gets a lot of support thanks to the sheer number of companion plugins, apps, and clients available for your media. However, Plex has been around longer and also has some must-have companion apps that make managing your media easier. From server monitoring to alternative playback apps and more, you'll likely find something you want to add to your Plex setup.

I finally found an open-source Plex client that feels better than the official app

Plezy is the Plex app that Plex should have built, and it's completely free

item.title: I stopped manually hunting for duplicate photos after finding this Synology tool
item.itunes:title: I stopped manually hunting for duplicate photos after finding this Synology tool
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've got hundreds of thousands of photos sitting on my Synology NAS, and the fact of the matter is that a significant portion of them are duplicates that I haven't gotten around to yet. Some are exact copies, while others might be compressed versions shared by others. There are even versions created during photo editing sessions. Finding them manually is just not practical. I simply don't have the time for it.

It's my search for a deduplication tool that led me to the annoyingly named dedupPictures. This app, as cryptic as it sounds, can talk directly to my Synology NAS instead of downloading every photo to my Mac, using the thumbnails that Synology already generates. It then compares them locally and gives me an easy interface where I can decide what stays and what gets deleted. It's helped me recover hundreds of gigabytes of space from my NAS.

I'm torn between these 5 user-friendly NAS image hosting tools

Spoilt for choice

1
By  Chandraveer Mathur

My Mac does the heavy lifting

It doesn't need to download the original photos

The big problem with deduplication tools tends to be the way that they access a NAS. If I mount my Synology over SMB, most tools need to pull down full-size images over the network to determine whether the two photos are the same. That's particularly inefficient when I have RAW files or large JPEGs. Downloading terabytes of data is just inefficient.

DedupPictures takes a better approach when deployed with a Synology NAS. It connects to Synology DSM's FileStation API and pulls down the NAS-generated thumbnails instead. Those thumbnails are obviously an order of magnitude smaller in size. Compared to the full images, you end up saving a huge amount of data, and the app works off these thumbnails to inspect the library without moving the full-resolution images across the network.

In fact, this is the biggest reason why I opted for the app. My photo library stays on the NAS, while my much faster Mac does the comparison work. I can point it at the relevant folder, let it scan the files, and get results without filling up my Mac's storage. And let me be real, I don't even have enough storage to pull it off on my Mac.

I get to choose what gets deleted

Perceptual hashing catches different versions

  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 

The other aspect that stands out is that the app doesn't rely just on exact file matching. It uses a perceptual hash that is designed to recognize photographs that look the same even when the files are not identical. It's this hashing algorithm that catches cases when an image has been resized, recompressed, or sent through WhatsApp and saved again.

This was particularly important to me as my photo library, stretching across hundreds of thousands of images, has been compiled over decades. Invariably, there are duplicate images, versions, compressed copies, and even files with differing file names. Just file name-based deduplication simply wouldn't work for me. For the file system, they are separate photos. But technically, they might be the same image.

DedupPictures maintains a cache of its hashes so that once you've scanned the library, you don't need to repeat the analysis with subsequent runs. It makes it particularly useful for longer projects where you want to maintain your library under control as new photos are added in.

Of course, finding duplicates is just one part of the problem. As good as the software is, I don't trust it to decide exactly which photos to delete. No algorithm is perfect, and an accidentally deleted photo is not acceptable.

Instead, dedupPictures gives me a local web interface where duplicate groups are displayed together. While it automatically selects a file to keep, favoring the larger of two or more files, you have the option of changing the selection. You can make all of these selections, hit delete, and let it handle the rest.

You'll also find a semantic mode that solves the problem of retakes. Perceptual hashing is great at recognizing copies of the same image, but it can't identify images that are close enough but slightly different. Instead, the app, when in semantic mode, uses a local CLIP vision model to compare what's depicted in the image.

This can be useful when cleaning up photos taken in burst mode and repeated shots. Often enough, while out and about, I'll capture multiple photos of the same subject to make sure I capture the frame. But I don't really need all these files. I only need the one or two images that captured the setting. The CLIP model can help identify all these images. It previews and reviews these images, and serves up the web server for you to choose the images to keep or delete.

The easiest way to keep my NAS photo library clean

Removing duplicate photos is a big part of maintaining a clean photo library. But more than that, in this economy, anything that saves me having to buy another hard drive by releasing wasted space is an essential tool.

DedupPictures handles my mess of a photo library elegantly by removing duplicate photos, copies, resized images, and much more. And it does this without having to pull down my entire image library from my NAS. That alone makes it a worthwhile addition to keeping my photo library clean.

dedupPictures : This photo deduplication tool finds duplicate and visually similar images to help you review and remove extra copies.

item.title: Here's why your Plex server feels slow even on Ethernet, and a $10 fix is the answer
item.itunes:title: Here's why your Plex server feels slow even on Ethernet, and a $10 fix is the answer
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Your home Wi-Fi is probably powered by a 300–500 Mbps internet plan, or even Gigabit speeds, but raw throughput is often not enough for stable Plex streaming. Your raw, uncompressed media running on a wireless connection can often experience sudden dips if something else in the house demands a burst of bandwidth. That's why Ethernet is preferred on TVs if you can route a cable to your media room.

However, another spanner in the works is the ancient 100 Mbps LAN port on most TVs, even in 2026. This bandwidth may be enough for Netflix streaming, but not always for lossless 4K Blu-ray remuxes. You need to bypass your TV's Ethernet port with a faster one if you want a rock-solid Plex (or Jellyfin) experience.

I thought my TV needed Ethernet, but Wi-Fi proved me wrong

Routing that cable wasn't worth the hassle.

By  Hamlin Rozario

You hardwired your TV, but your Plex stream is still not perfect

Local lossless media can exceed your TV's LAN capabilities

Wi-Fi speeds have reached multi-gig standards in many parts of the world. Even if you have a 300 Mbps connection like most US homes, it's considerably faster than what you need for conventional streaming. Apps like Netflix compress the stream significantly, bringing it down to around 25 Mbps, allowing almost any internet plan to support it. Local media enthusiasts running a Plex or Jellyfin server, however, often need a lot more bandwidth.

Uncompressed 4K Blu-ray files can demand peak bandwidth of up to 200 Mbps if you factor in occasional spikes. Your Wi-Fi may be fast enough to accommodate this bandwidth, but it'll never be as stable as a wired connection. Ethernet removes the myriad of wireless complexities linked to congestion and interference, giving your TV a direct line to the server.

The problem is that most TVs still feature a 100 Mbps Ethernet port. Even if your Plex server is wired directly to the TV, you can still encounter buffering when the stream shoots past 100 Mbps. You may wonder why the supposedly flawless Ethernet connection is letting you down, but the issue is simply the dated hardware of your TV.

Your home server needs Ethernet, but not for the reason you think

Stability over speed, always.

1
By  Samir Makwana

A cheap Ethernet adapter is your way out

All the benefits of Ethernet without your TV's constraints

Your friend might recommend buying a separate streaming box to enjoy faster Ethernet capabilities, but you don't need to spend that much if you just want a faster Ethernet port. A USB-to-Ethernet adapter can provide you with a Gigabit LAN port for under $10, and it's usually plug-and-play with most LG, Sony, and Android/Google TVs.

This cheap and simple adapter allows your server to transmit your local media at Gigabit speeds, as long as your TV has a USB 3.0 port. Older TVs might have USB 2.0 instead, but even that's capable of a theoretical 480 Mbps connection with your media server. Even if you get real-world LAN speeds of around 300–400 Mbps, that's at least triple what you were getting before, and more than enough for running any 4K Blu-ray remux.

TP-Link USB to Ethernet Adapter
See at Amazon
Your TV's Ethernet port might be slower than its Wi-Fi connection, but it actually doesn't matter

Use the port wisely.

12
By  Samir Makwana

TV manufacturers ought to move on from 100 Mbps LAN ports

It's been nearly three decades since Gigabit Ethernet came out, yet TV brands still haven't adopted it as a standard feature. While it's true that most people will never saturate the 100 Mbps cap on their TV's LAN port, it's high time Gigabit ports became commonplace on TVs. They became the minimum on budget motherboards years ago; there's no reason for expensive TVs to stick to legacy LAN ports anymore.
